A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same problem-oriented code-optimization work, although v2 substantially revises its second contribution. All pages, including equations, tables, figures, and appendices, were available for inspection.

before.justification: V1 reports original prompting, fine-tuning, model-merging, optimization-type, and error-analysis results, including Tables 2–4 and Figures 3 and 5.

after.justification: V2 reports original fine-tuning and anchor-verification experiments, structural and semantic analyses, data-efficiency experiments, and appendix case studies.

M1.justification: V1 addresses correctness bottlenecks by merging models separately fine-tuned on user-oriented and problem-oriented pairs using Merge-Linear or Merge-Slerp. V2 replaces this with anchor verification: generate test inputs, execute the original slow code to obtain reference outputs, and refine optimized code using execution feedback. This substantially changes inference.

E1.justification: Both versions train and evaluate on CodeNet/PIE-derived C++ competitive-programming code with execution-time optimization as the task. PCO continues the problem-oriented reconstruction of PIE. Changed pair selection, counts, and partitions remain within this coverage; no additional domain, language, or independent benchmark is evaluated.

E2.justification: The correctness-improvement comparisons drop Curriculum-Learning and add Direct Test Generation, while retaining the self-correction comparison family as Self-Debugging. Prompt comparisons also remove GPT-3.5 and CodeLlama 34B. V2 adds Qwen2.5-Coder comparisons against PIE fine-tuning controls, substantially revising the evaluated comparison set.

E3.justification: V1 selects problem-oriented pairs with greater than 90% runtime reduction; v2 selects top-speedup pairs while matching PIE's pair count per problem. Training sets change from 56,086/14,051 pairs to 77,967 each, and the test set changes from 1,422 samples across 80 problems to 978 across 41. Model configurations and LoRA targets also change. New refinement experiments cap methods at one iteration, with three generated inputs or cases for test-based methods.

E4.justification: V2 adds CFG graph-edit-distance analysis, semantic-embedding visualization, training-data percentage experiments, and three anchor-verification case studies. It also examines refinement benefits on PIE versus PCO. V1's merge-weight sensitivity study and failure-category breakdown disappear. The original optimization-type analysis and four illustrative code comparisons are retained, with the latter relocated to Figures 15–18.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. BEST@1/BEST@8 remains a candidate-selection protocol rather than uncertainty estimation. The human and GPT-4 sampling counts remain 100 and 1,000 pairs, respectively.

E6.justification: Many retained-model results are replaced: DeepSeek-Coder 33B's problem-oriented BEST@8 results change from 71.03% optimized and 4.812× speedup in v1 to 74.87% and 6.67× in v2, under changed settings. V2 adds anchor-verification results, including 58.90% to 71.06% optimized, 5.22× to 6.08× speedup, and 61.55% to 74.54% correctness with DeepSeek-V3 refinement. V1's merging and error-breakdown results are removed.

T1.justification: V2 Section 3.1 adds explicit combinatorial pair-count expressions under assumptions about numbers of problems, users, and submissions, supporting an additional scaling argument. V1 describes trajectories, pairs, and filtering thresholds without this counting argument. No substantial theorem or proof development is added.

C1.justification: The central claim that problem-oriented pairs improve code optimization remains. However, v1's main contribution of overcoming correctness bottlenecks through model merging is replaced by anchor verification mitigating the 'optimization tax.' Correctness improvement becomes an explicit central contribution alongside optimization ratio and speedup.

C2.justification: V2 replaces merging and curriculum-learning explanations with interpretations about structural diversity, data efficiency, and reliable test outputs from slow code. Its limitations replace the natural-language-to-efficient-code research question with unresolved full correctness. One new interpretation overstates PCO's optimization-ratio advantage: Tables 2 and 4 report DeepSeek-V3 refinement gains of 12.16 percentage points on PCO versus 16.04 on PIE, although the speedup gain is larger on PCO.

D1.justification: V2 adds LLAMA-FACTORY and vLLM usage, model-version and base-versus-chat details, explicit anchor-verification and comparator prompts, and a concrete code-access URL. Reported hardware changes from four to eight A100 GPUs, and LoRA targets change from q_proj/v_proj to all. V1's average test-case counts and performance-conditioned-generation documentation are omitted.

R1.justification: V2 introduces substantial positioning against generated-test and execution-filtering approaches, citing CodeT, B4, and SelfCodeAlign to motivate anchor verification. Model-soup and curriculum-learning positioning disappears. References also expand to newer code models, code-efficiency research, and tools supporting the new analyses.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and dataset-construction explanation are extensively rewritten. Previously separate experimental-setting, results, and analysis sections are reorganized into Section 3, followed by the anchor-verification section. Appendices are substantially reorganized, with training details, prompts, and retained examples moved into a new structure.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn as submission trajectories, and the optimization-type pie charts become separate human and LLM bar charts. V2 adds structural, semantic, data-efficiency, verification-framework, prompt, and case-study displays, plus comparison tables with delta columns. Dataset statistics move to the appendix, and retained code examples become Figures 15–18.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for the central claim by matching training pair counts per problem, addressing v1's unequal data-size and problem-coverage comparison, and adding structural and data-efficiency analyses. Anchor verification is documented concretely and tested against self-debugging and direct test generation across three backbones, providing stronger evidence for its correctness mechanism. Some new PIE/PCO interpretations overstate the reported optimization-ratio gains, but the improved controls and methodological evidence provide a substantial net benefit. Changed splits prevent treating higher cross-version scores as directly comparable performance gains.
